books.section: Topic 4.6 Market Revolution: Society and Culture, D. Gender and Family Roles in the Age of the Market Revolution

primary_sources: Catharine Beecher, A Treatise on Domestic Economy (1841)

stimulus.text: Catharine Beecher, A Treatise on Domestic Economy (1841): “In this Country, it is established, both by opinion and by practice, that women have an equal interest in all social and civil concerns; and that no domestic, civil, or political, institution is right, that sacrifices her interest to promote that of the other sex. But in order to secure her the more firmly in all these privileges, it is decided, that in the domestic relation, she take a subordinate station, and that, in civil and political concerns, her interests be intrusted to the other sex, without her taking any part in voting, or in making and administering laws.” Beecher added that “the formation of the moral and intellectual character of the young is committed mainly to the female hand.”
stimulus.source_note: Catharine Beecher, A Treatise on Domestic Economy (1841), Chapter 1. Verbatim quotations verified against the Project Gutenberg text (eBook 21829) and the Columbia University transcription.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Beecher's argument that women should run the home while men run public life best reflects which idea of the period?

options.text: Republican motherhood, which asked women to raise virtuous citizens
options.misconception: Republican motherhood gave women's child-raising a public purpose; Beecher keeps women out of public life, which is the newer domestic ideal.

options.text: The free-labor ideology, which praised wage work as a path to independence
options.misconception: Free labor is about wage earners rising to independence; Beecher is about women's place in the home, not about wages.

options.text: The temperance movement, which blamed drink for family poverty
options.misconception: Temperance fought alcohol; Beecher's subject is where women belong, not drink.

options.text: The cult of domesticity, which made the home a woman's separate sphere

rationales.A: Republican motherhood came after the Revolution and asked women to raise citizens for public life. Beecher's ideal is less public: women stay out of voting and lawmaking.
rationales.B: The free-labor idea praises wage work as a road to owning land. Beecher praises housework, not wage work, as women's road to influence.
rationales.C: Temperance aimed at drink. Beecher aims at defining women's sphere, a different cause with different means.
rationales.D: Beecher assigns women to the home and keeps them from voting and lawmaking, while praising their power over the young. That separate sphere, with the home as women's place, is the cult of domesticity.
rationales.general:
1. Name what Beecher divides. Home for women, public life for men, with no crossing over.
2. Test the older idea. Republican motherhood also praised mothers, but it tied them to public life, not away from it.
3. Name the newer idea. A separate home sphere for women is the cult of domesticity.
Background: Republican motherhood gave way to the cult of domesticity in the early nineteenth century, as work moved out of the home and into factories and offices.
Remember: two ideas can praise the same people for opposite reasons, so check what each one asks them to do.
